title: Escalation Drill
subtitle: 3-year-old with worsening bronchiolitis — from nasal prongs to high flow
stem: Night shift on the paediatric ward, 1:10 am. Aarav, 3 years, was admitted at 6 pm with bronchiolitis on nasal prongs 2 L/min. You are the ward nurse; the resident is in the emergency room with another child.
parent: "He was better at 10 o'clock. Now he's breathing so fast and making that noise again. He won't settle, he keeps pushing me away."

vitals.note: On nasal prongs 2 L/min. Marked subcostal and intercostal recessions, tracheal tug, intermittent grunting. Widespread wheeze and crackles. Agitated, pushes the mask away. Chest still moving well.

decisions.title: Impression

options.text: Unstable, non-life-threatening — mild distress; turn the prongs up and recheck at the 2 am round
options.outcome: Prongs turned up to 3 L/min. At 1:40 am he is grunting louder: SpO₂ 88 %, RR 60.
options.note: Grunting, tracheal tug and SpO₂ 90 % on oxygen are not mild. Grunting is the child generating his own PEEP: a sign of impending failure. Fifty minutes unobserved is dangerous.

options.text: Unstable — severe respiratory distress with impending respiratory failure; escalate now
options.outcome: You press the call bell for the resident and stay with him.
options.note: Effort is maximal, efficacy is failing despite oxygen, and agitation is an early effect of hypoxaemia. He is still compensating, which is exactly when escalation prevents failure.

options.text: Unstable, life-threatening — respiratory failure; bag-mask ventilate now
options.outcome: You start bagging. He is awake and fights the mask; his own breaths clash with yours. HR 170 and he is more agitated.
options.note: He is breathing hard, awake, agitated and moving his chest well. That is impending failure, not failure. Bagging an awake, vigorously breathing child is ineffective and distressing. Escalate support, prepare the bag, keep watching.

options.text: Not a breathing problem — he is anxious about the hospital
options.outcome: Lights dimmed, his mother in a chair. Fifteen minutes later he is still grunting: SpO₂ 87 %, HR 160.
options.note: Agitation in a hypoxaemic child is the hypoxaemia. Comfort measures are good; they are not the treatment.

must: severe respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure

decisions.title: Intervention
decisions.prompt: You have called for the resident. What is your intervention for his breathing?

options.text: Increase nasal prongs to 4 L/min
options.outcome: At 4 L/min he rubs at his nose and cries; the gas is cold and dry. SpO₂ stays at 90 %, RR 60.
options.note: Standard nasal prongs above 2 L/min in a child give dry, cold gas and little extra FiO₂; the nose will not tolerate it. He needs a step up, not more of the same.

options.text: Start HFNC at 2 L/kg/min (about 28 L/min), FiO₂ 0.4–0.6, heated and humidified, titrated to SpO₂ 94–98 % — with a non-rebreather mask as a bridge while the circuit is set up

vitals.note: On HFNC 28 L/min FiO₂ 0.5 after 20 minutes. Grunting stopped. Recessions less.

options.outcome: Non-rebreather on while you assemble the HFNC circuit. Twenty minutes on 28 L/min, FiO₂ 0.5: the grunting stops and the recessions ease.
options.note: HFNC flushes dead space, gives a PEEP-like effect and warms and humidifies the gas; it is the next step for moderate–severe bronchiolitis. Set up per your unit protocol; the non-rebreather bridges the few minutes of assembly.

options.text: Non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min and continue observing on the ward

vitals.note: SpO₂ up but still grunting and recessing.

options.outcome: On the non-rebreather SpO₂ climbs to 96 % — but he is still grunting and recessing at RR 56.
options.note: A reasonable bridge, but not the destination. A non-rebreather gives high FiO₂ with no flow support, so the work of breathing does not fall. If SpO₂ improves but the recessions and grunting do not, he is still heading for failure.

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol and wait for the response
options.outcome: Nebuliser running. Fifteen minutes later SpO₂ 89 %, HR 168, no change in his effort.
options.note: Bronchodilators have no consistent benefit in bronchiolitis, and a nebuliser does not treat hypoxaemia with impending failure. If your protocol allows a trial, it must not delay the escalation of oxygen support.

decisions.key: Escalate respiratory support: HFNC at about 2 L/kg/min, heated and humidified, FiO2 titrated to SpO2 94–98 %, with a non-rebreather mask as a bridge while it is set up.

decisions.title: Reassessment
decisions.label: Your reassessment
decisions.prompt: One hour on HFNC 28 L/min, FiO₂ 0.5. Reassess him: is it working, and what do you do now?

opts.v: Check HR and RR are falling and SpO₂ is 94–98 %
Wean the flow to 10 L/min now that he is better
Check work of breathing: grunting, recessions, tracheal tug
Check the circuit: prongs less than half the nostril, humidifier on, water chamber filled
Turn FiO₂ to 1.0 to be safe overnight
Score PEWS and chart it
Start oral feeds now that he is comfortable
Pass a nasogastric tube; nil by mouth for now

options.text: Check HR and RR are falling and SpO₂ is 94–98 %; Check work of breathing: grunting, recessions, tracheal tug; Check the circuit: prongs less than half the nostril, humidifier on, water chamber filled
options.outcome: HR 130, RR 44, SpO₂ 96 % on FiO₂ 0.45; no grunting, mild recessions. The prongs fit well and the humidifier is at 37 °C. HFNC is working.
options.note: A fall in HR and RR in the first 1–2 hours is the sign of response. Then the nursing checks — prongs, humidity, feeds, position — keep him safe overnight.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: Part of the picture is checked. At 3 am the prongs have slipped and he is grunting again: RR 54, SpO₂ 92 %.

options.text: Wean the flow to 10 L/min now that he is better
options.outcome: Flow weaned to 10 L/min. Within 40 minutes RR is 54, SpO₂ 91 %, and the recessions are back.

options.text: Turn FiO₂ to 1.0 to be safe overnight
options.outcome: FiO₂ turned to 1.0. The monitor reads 100 % — and will keep reading high even as he tires.

options.text: Start oral feeds now that he is comfortable
options.outcome: He takes a few sips of milk, coughs and splutters. SpO₂ dips to 89 % and he is breathing faster.

decisions.title: Communication with the parents
decisions.label: Your communication with the mother
decisions.prompt: His mother looks at the machine: “Sister, what is this big machine? Is he going to the ICU?”

opts.v: Explain simply: warm, moist air with oxygen that helps him breathe with less effort
“Don’t ask questions now, I am busy”
Tell her what you are watching and that you will check him every hour
Give her a job: keep him calm on her lap, no milk by mouth, call you if the prongs slip
“He will be fine by morning”
Be honest: if he does not improve, he may need the PICU

options.text: Explain simply: warm, moist air with oxygen that helps him breathe with less effort; Tell her what you are watching and that you will check him every hour; Give her a job: keep him calm on her lap, no milk by mouth, call you if the prongs slip
options.outcome: She holds him upright on her lap and he falls asleep. At 3 am she calls you because a prong has slipped — you fix it before his saturation falls.
options.note: Explain the machine in plain words, say what you are watching, and give the parent a safe job at the bedside.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: She stays quiet and anxious. At 2:30 am she gives him a bottle of milk to settle him; he coughs and his saturation dips to 91 %.

options.text: “Don’t ask questions now, I am busy”
options.outcome: Frightened, she keeps lifting the prongs to look at his nose; each time his saturation dips.

options.text: “He will be fine by morning”
options.outcome: At 4 am he needs more oxygen and the doctor talks of the PICU. The mother is angry: “You said he would be fine.”

decisions.title: Team communication
decisions.label: Your communication with the team
decisions.prompt: The resident is still in the emergency room. How do you communicate with the team?

opts.v: ISBAR to the resident with numbers: grunting, SpO₂ 90 % on 2 L, RR 58; now on HFNC 28 L/min, FiO₂ 0.5, RR 48
Agree when to escalate: HR/RR not falling in 1–2 hours or FiO₂ above 0.6 → call the PICU
“Sir, the child is serious” — with no numbers
Read back the HFNC settings you are given
Tell the charge nurse he needs closer nursing (1:2)
Note it in the file and tell the morning team

options.text: ISBAR to the resident with numbers: grunting, SpO₂ 90 % on 2 L, RR 58; now on HFNC 28 L/min, FiO₂ 0.5, RR 48; Agree when to escalate: HR/RR not falling in 1–2 hours or FiO₂ above 0.6 → call the PICU; Read back the HFNC settings you are given
options.outcome: The resident confirms the settings, reviews him at 2 am and informs the PICU registrar. Everyone knows when to call.
options.note: ISBAR with numbers, a read-back of the settings, and escalation triggers agreed in advance.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: The resident knows he is on high flow, but nobody has said when to escalate; by 4 am the FiO₂ has crept up to 0.7 before anyone calls.

options.text: “Sir, the child is serious” — with no numbers
options.outcome: The resident asks you to “keep watching”. Nobody senior reviews him for two hours.

options.text: Note it in the file and tell the morning team
options.outcome: At 7 am the day team finds him grunting on FiO₂ 0.8, which had crept up overnight.

decisions.title: Transfer
decisions.label: Your transfer plan
decisions.prompt: The resident asks where he should be looked after for the rest of the night.

opts.v: HDU/PICU — continuous SpO₂ monitoring and 1:2 nursing for a child on HFNC
Stay on the general ward with 4-hourly observations
Move him on HFNC or a non-rebreather with a full portable cylinder, monitor, bag-mask and suction
A trained nurse escorts him and hands over with ISBAR
His mother goes with him; his notes and charts go too
Send him to the PICU with the ward attendant

options.text: HDU/PICU — continuous SpO₂ monitoring and 1:2 nursing for a child on HFNC; Move him on HFNC or a non-rebreather with a full portable cylinder, monitor, bag-mask and suction; A trained nurse escorts him and hands over with ISBAR
options.outcome: He moves to the HDU on HFNC, monitored, with you beside him and his mother following. The HDU nurse takes the ISBAR handover and he sleeps.
options.note: A child on HFNC needs HDU-level monitoring. Move him with oxygen, monitoring, airway kit and a trained escort.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: The move happens, but not every piece was in place; he arrives with the monitor off and is unwatched for several minutes.

options.text: Stay on the general ward with 4-hourly observations
options.outcome: At the 4 am check he is grunting on FiO₂ 0.7, RR 64 — nobody had looked since midnight.

options.text: Send him to the PICU with the ward attendant
options.outcome: In the lift the cylinder runs low and the attendant cannot read the monitor; he arrives with SpO₂ 85 %.

debrief: Which of the 3 E’s told you this was impending failure rather than distress?
What signs in the first 1–2 hours told you HFNC was working, and what would have told you it was failing?
Which nursing checks keep a child safe on high flow overnight?
takeHome: Grunting, SpO₂ falling on oxygen and agitation = impending failure: escalate while the child is still compensating.
HFNC at 2 L/kg/min is the step after nasal prongs; bridge with a non-rebreather while setting up.
Response to HFNC shows in HR and RR within 1–2 hours; the nursing care keeps it safe.
If HFNC fails — rising RR and HR, falling SpO₂, drowsiness or apnoea — escalate: bag-mask at 1 breath every 2–3 s and call the intensivist.
references: AHA PALS Provider Manual 2020: respiratory distress and failure, rescue breathing rates (1 breath every 2–3 s), bag-mask technique.
IAP ICC PCCN Module 02: 3 E's, oxygen delivery devices, HFNC, bag-mask ventilation.

ending.smooth: He stays on HFNC in the HDU overnight. By the morning his HR and RR have settled and the FiO₂ is down to 0.3. His mother was kept informed throughout.
ending.detour: He reaches the HDU, but after a longer spell of hypoxaemia; he needs a PICU review and a higher FiO₂ through the night.
